candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the property name or property path passed to BeanUtils/PropertyUtils, or the map key passed to BeanMap.get()/containsKey(). If an application wraps a bean in BeanMap, passes the BeanMap to BeanUtils/PropertyUtils property APIs, or otherwise lets untrusted keys reach the BeanMap Map interface, the attacker can request the key "class".
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The default PropertyUtilsBean and BeanUtilsBean do suppress "class": resetBeanIntrospectors() installs DefaultBeanIntrospector plus SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector.SUPPRESS_CLASS, and BeanUtilsBean.copyProperties() explicitly skips a descriptor named "class" for standard bean origins. Direct BeanUtilsBean.getProperty(bean, "class") on the underlying bean therefore fails as documented. The issue is specifically the BeanMap Map interface and Map-first resolution path. BeanMap is an opt-in API, so ordinary applications that never use BeanMap or never pass it to BeanUtils are unaffected. Exploitability beyond disclosure depends on JDK/container versions and reachable chains; modern JDKs may block reflective access to ClassLoader internals. No runtime validation was performed.
candidates.impact: Bypasses the default suppression of the class property, disclosing Class and ClassLoader objects and potentially allowing traversal or modification of class-loader state. In applications with a suitable object graph and writable properties, this is the CVE-2014-0114-style class-loader manipulation pattern and can lead to remote code execution or container compromise; where no writable chain is reachable, it is at least a sensitive class/class-loader disclosure and an access-control bypass.
candidates.prerequisites: The application must use BeanMap over a normal bean and expose untrusted property names to BeanMap or pass the BeanMap as the bean/Map to BeanUtils/PropertyUtils. Normal PropertyUtilsBean/BeanUtilsBean use on the underlying bean alone blocks "class". For the strongest impact (class-loader state traversal or CVE-2014-0114-style exploitation), there must also be reachable getter/setter chains on the returned Class/ClassLoader objects; modern JDK/container versions may restrict parts of such chains. Without such a chain, the confirmed impact is an access-control bypass exposing Class and ClassLoader objects.
candidates.root_cause: BeanMap.initialize() obtains property descriptors with the raw JDK Introspector and unconditionally stores every readable property, including the synthetic "class" property backed by Object.getClass(). It never consults SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector, unlike PropertyUtilsBean, whose resetBeanIntrospectors() installs SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector.SUPPRESS_CLASS by default. Because BeanMap also implements Map, PropertyUtilsBean.getNestedProperty()/BeanUtilsBean.setProperty() treat it as a dynamic map and resolve attacker-supplied keys such as "class" directly through BeanMap.get(), bypassing the normal JavaBean introspection path where "class" is suppressed.
candidates.title: BeanMap exposes the suppressed class property and enables class-loader path traversal
candidates.trace: 1) new BeanMap(someBean) invokes initialize(), which calls Introspector.getBeanInfo(beanClass) and puts every readable property, including "class" -> Object.getClass(), into readMethods (BeanMap.java 468-499). 2) BeanMap.get("class") looks up that method and invokes it, returning a Class object (BeanMap.java 380-393). 3) BeanMap implements Map, so PropertyUtilsBean.getNestedProperty() takes the bean instanceof Map branch for the first path segment and calls getPropertyOfMapBean(map, "class"), which simply returns map.get("class") (PropertyUtilsBean.java 571-603, 784-799). The default SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector is therefore never consulted for that segment. 4) After the first segment, the returned Class object is introspected normally. Suppression only removes the property named "class"; properties such as "classLoader" (Class.getClassLoader()) remain readable, so a path such as class.classLoader... can continue to ClassLoader state. 5) The same Map-first resolution occurs in BeanUtilsBean.setProperty()/PropertyUtilsBean.setNestedProperty(), so writable class-loader chains can be reached in the classic property-injection pattern.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no tests exist in the visible snapshot, so the BeanMap behavior and the class.classLoader trace are source-derived, not runtime-confirmed. The exact exploitability of any ClassLoader chain depends on the application, JDK, and container. The mapping to any externally assigned CVE identifier was intentionally not checked in this run.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Access Control / Security Control Bypass

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned 157 model-visible files: repository metadata/build/site files and all 121 main Java source files. Binary-like files were skipped by the tool filter (0 reported), no sensitive-name/path exclusions or symlink exclusions were reported, and there are no src/test files in the snapshot. Search and reading covered BeanMap, PropertyUtilsBean, BeanUtilsBean, SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector, BeanIntrospectionData, DefaultIntrospectionContext, FluentPropertyBeanIntrospector, MethodUtils, ConstructorUtils, expression resolvers, converters, locale support, DynaBean implementations, and JDBC support classes. The strongest source-supported issue is the BeanMap class-property suppression bypass.
limitations: No code, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed; all conclusions are static source analysis and no finding is runtime-confirmed.
The snapshot contains no src/test directory, so there are no repository tests to validate BeanMap's exposure of the class property or to confirm suppression behavior across JDK versions.
Exploitability depends on application usage: BeanMap must be used or passed to BeanUtils/PropertyUtils with untrusted keys, and stronger impact requires a reachable writable ClassLoader chain.
Modern JDK module and reflection restrictions may prevent parts of the historical ClassLoader traversal, so the practical RCE risk could be lower than the historical CVE-2014-0114 pattern.

External advisories, CVE/CWE mappings, patches, and sibling-repository data were intentionally not consulted, so the candidate is an independent source-based lead rather than a confirmed advisory match.
Only readable text files exposed by the tools were inspected; generated, binary, and any non-visible artifacts were not available.

rejected_leads.lead: PropertyUtilsBean.getPropertyDescriptor() falls back to new MappedPropertyDescriptor(name, bean.getClass()) after suppression removes a descriptor, so a suppressed "class" name could be recreated.
rejected_leads.reason: The mapped-descriptor fallback requires the bean class to expose a mapped accessor such as getClass(String) or setClass(String, ...). That is not a universal JavaBean shape and no such path is provided by Object/Class itself, so this is not the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: FluentPropertyBeanIntrospector is appended after SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector and can recreate a descriptor for a suppressed property name if a bean has a matching set method.
rejected_leads.reason: It requires explicit addition of FluentPropertyBeanIntrospector by the application and can only create a write-only descriptor for "class" (null read method), so it does not restore the readable getClass path or preserve the broad BeanMap bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: ClassConverter converts attacker-controlled strings to Class objects by loading them from the thread context class loader.
rejected_leads.reason: The converter is designed for that operation, loading does not initialize the class, and exploitation requires an application target property of type Class or a setter that performs a dangerous action. No direct source path from untrusted input to code execution was established.

rejected_leads.lead: InetAddressConverter performs InetAddress.getByName(value) and can trigger DNS resolution for attacker-controlled values.
rejected_leads.reason: The behavior is inherent to the converter, requires an InetAddress-typed destination property, and at most gives DNS lookup/SSRF-like side effects rather than the class-loader access-control bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: JDBC DynaClass implementations load column classes named by result-set metadata and Class.forName is used in AbstractJdbcDynaClass.
rejected_leads.reason: Class names come from JDBC metadata/driver behavior rather than ordinary untrusted request input, and the loaded class is not initialized (Class.forName(..., false, ...)). This is a weaker trust boundary than the BeanMap path.

summary: One candidate submitted: BeanMap bypasses the library's default SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector and exposes the synthetic "class" property (Object.getClass()), providing a route to Class/ClassLoader objects even though PropertyUtilsBean and BeanUtilsBean suppress that property by default. The strongest source trace is BeanMap.initialize() registering getClass as a readable property, then BeanMap.get("class") returning Class through the Map interface, and PropertyUtilsBean.getNestedProperty() treating any Map as a dynamic source and fetching map keys directly. Other observed leads (mapped-descriptor fallback, FluentPropertyBeanIntrospector re-adding a write-only class descriptor, ClassConverter class loading, InetAddressConverter DNS resolution, JDBC metadata class loading) are weaker and are listed as rejected leads rather than additional candidates.
